subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Trust Game
description: A 60-second lesson on The Trust Game.

hook.text: You send $5 to a stranger. The amount triples to $15. The stranger decides how much to return. Rationally: nothing.

buildup.text: The trust game measures trust via sending money and trustworthiness via returning it.

discovery.text: Berg's experiment showed most people send about half and recipients return about a third.

twist.text: Oxytocin increases trust. Participants given oxytocin nasal spray sent markedly more money.

climax.text: Trust is an economic lubricant. Countries with higher trust levels have higher GDP.

punchline.text: Trust pays off. Not always, but on average, always.

quiz.question: What does the trust game measure?
options: How quickly people make financial decisions
Trust through money sent and trustworthiness through money returned
Whether people prefer gambling over saving

details.summary: The trust game measures interpersonal trust by having one player send money that gets multiplied, and the receiver decides how much to return. Trust levels and reciprocity rates vary by culture but averaging around 50 percent is sent and 30 percent returned.
details.whyItMatters: Trust is the foundation of economic exchange. The trust game quantifies how much people are willing to risk based on expected reciprocity, revealing that societies with higher trust levels enjoy greater economic prosperity.
takeaways: Senders typically trust about 50 percent of their endowment
Receivers return roughly one-third of the multiplied amount
Higher national trust levels correlate with greater economic growth

faq.question: Why do people trust strangers in the trust game?
faq.answer: Expectations of reciprocity, social norms around fairness, risk tolerance, and optimism about human nature all contribute. People with higher general trust in society tend to send more, and their trust is often justified by reciprocal returns.

faq.question: What factors increase trust in the game?
faq.answer: Face-to-face interaction, shared group identity, communication before the game, and growing up in high-trust societies all increase the amount sent. Betrayal experience and anonymity decrease trust.
